## 1. What you'll build, and why

For thirty-two concepts every program has ended the same way: SIL → IRGen → **LLVM IR** → `clang` →
native. LLVM did the last mile — instruction selection, register allocation, scheduling, encoding.
This phase takes that last mile away and builds it **ourselves**, in OCaml, targeting **ARM64**
(AArch64, Apple Silicon). By the end of Phase 8 we have *two* backends sharing one front end: the
LLVM spine (Backend A) and a from-scratch native compiler (Backend B).

This concept is the first step: **instruction selection** — turning each SIL operation into ARM64
machine instructions. v0 is deliberately the simplest thing that works: a **stack machine**. Every
SIL value gets a slot in the function's stack frame; each instruction loads its operands into
scratch registers, computes, and stores the result back. It's correct, it runs real `fib` and loops
and prints, it matches `swiftc` — and it's *slow*, because every value lives in memory. That
slowness is the entire motivation for concept 34 (register allocation), which keeps values in
registers and makes the load/store traffic disappear.

- **You implement:** `sel_instr` (the per-SIL-op ARM64 templates) and `sel_term` (the branch/return
  terminators) — the "munch" that maps SIL onto the machine.
- **Outcome:** `swiftml8 build x.swift --native` produces a real ARM64 executable that runs and
  matches `swiftc` on the scalar + control-flow + functions corpus.

> **New to ARM64?** A few facts used below. There are 31 general registers `x0`–`x30` (64-bit);
> `x0`–`x7` pass arguments and return values; `x9`–`x15` are caller-saved scratch; `sp` is the
> stack pointer; `x30` is the link register (the return address). Most instructions are
> `op dst, src1, src2`. There's no memory-to-memory: you `ldr` into a register, compute, `str`
> back. Apple prefixes symbols with `_` (`main` → `_main`).

## 2. Concepts in depth

### Instruction selection: SIL op → machine instructions

A SIL instruction like `%11 = binop "+" %9, %10` is *abstract* — it names values, not registers or
memory. Instruction selection picks concrete ARM64 instructions that realize it. The cleanest
possible scheme, and our v0, is the **stack machine**:

![The v0 stack machine. Each SIL value gets a stack-frame slot; a `binop add` lowers to: load both operands into scratch registers (`ldr x9` / `ldr x10`), compute (`add x9, x9, x10`), store the result back (`str x9`). One template per SIL op. The load/store traffic is the cost — concept 34's register allocator removes it by keeping values in registers.](figs/isel.png)

Read the figure. `%9 = load %a` becomes `ldr x9, [sp, #off_a]; str x9, [sp, #off_9]`. The binop
becomes load-load-compute-store. Every value round-trips through memory. This is the same idea as a
naive bytecode interpreter's stack — hence "stack machine" — and it has one great virtue: it's
**local**. Each SIL instruction lowers in isolation, needing no knowledge of what's live, what's in
which register, or what comes next. That locality is why it's the right v0: get *correct* code out,
then optimize.

### The IR you consume, and the IR you emit

This concept adds no syntax — the language is exactly concept 32's. What is new is the
*target* IR. So instead of a grammar, here is the recall of both sides of the translation.

The **input** is raw (`-Onone`) SIL, the same form concept 09 hands to LLVM. Written as EBNF
(`[ x ]` optional, `{ x }` zero-or-more, `|` alternatives, quoted terminals), the fragment
your templates must cover is:

```
func    ::= "sil" "@" name "(" { value ":" type } ")" "->" type "{" { block } "}"
block   ::= "bb" int ":" { instr } term
instr   ::= [ value "=" ] op
op      ::= "integer_literal" type "," literal        (* Bool literals print this way too *)
          | "function_ref" "@" name
          | "alloc_stack" type | "load" value type | "store" value "to" value
          | "unop" '"-"' value | "binop" binop value "," value type
          | "apply" ( value | "@" name ) "(" { value } ")"
term    ::= "return" [ value ] | "br" "bb" int
          | "cond_br" value "," "bb" int "," "bb" int
          | "trap" | "unreachable"
binop   ::= '"+"' | '"-"' | '"*"' | '"/"' | '"%"'
          | '"=="' | '"!="' | '"<"' | '"<="' | '">"' | '">="'
```

(`print(x)` prints as `apply @print(%x)`, but it is its own SIL instruction, not a call:
`sel_instr` sees `Sil.Print`. `Sil.Binop` also admits `&&` and `||`, but SILGen lowers the
short-circuiting source operators to branch diamonds, so those two never reach you here.)

Every other SIL op — `struct`, `enum`, `alloc_ref`, `apply_witness`, the array intrinsics —
is outside v0's scope and takes the `; UNSUPPORTED` path below.

The **output** is `arm64.ml`, and all of it is new here:

| ARM64 form | what it does | |
|---|---|---|
| `mov` / `movz` / `movk` | move a register or build a 64-bit constant, 16 bits at a time | `<-- new` |
| `add` `sub` `mul` `sdiv` `msub` `neg` `and` `orr` | the integer ALU (`msub` synthesizes `%`) | `<-- new` |
| `cmp` / `cset` / `csel` | set the flags; materialize a Bool from them; select on them | `<-- new` |
| `ldr` / `str` / `stp` / `ldp` | load, store, and the pair forms the frame record uses | `<-- new` |
| `adrp` / `add …@PAGEOFF` | the PC-relative pair that addresses a string constant | `<-- new` |
| `b` / `b.<cond>` / `bl` / `ret` | branch, conditional branch, call, return | `<-- new` |
| `brk #1` | trap — SIGTRAP, exit 133 | `<-- new` |
| `Label` / `Comment` | a branch target; a `; …` line (this is where `UNSUPPORTED` goes) | `<-- new` |

Registers are `X n`, `SP` and `XZR`; the fourth constructor, `Virt n`, is reserved for concept
34's allocator and the printer refuses it, so v0 must only ever emit physical registers.

### The stack frame

Each function gets a frame, carved by adjusting `sp`. Our layout keeps `sp` **fixed for the whole
body** so that shuffling call arguments never disturbs slot offsets:

```
[sp, #0  .. #15]     outgoing call scratch (printf's variadic argument)
[sp, #16 .. ]        locals: SIL value %v lives at [sp, #16 + 8*v]
[sp, #LOCALS ..]     saved x29 (frame pointer) / x30 (link register) — the frame record
LOCALS = round16(16 + 8 * nvals)        (the whole frame is LOCALS + 16 bytes)
```

The **prologue** pushes the frame record *first*, then carves the locals:

```
sub  sp, sp, #16            ; room for the record
stp  x29, x30, [sp, #0]     ; save the caller's frame pointer and our return address
mov  x29, sp                ; x29 now points at the record (the AAPCS64 frame chain)
sub  sp, sp, #LOCALS        ; the slots
```

and the **epilogue** reverses it: `add sp, sp, #LOCALS; ldp x29, x30, [sp, #0]; add sp, sp, #16;
ret`. Why two `sub`s instead of one `sub sp, sp, #FRAME` followed by `stp x29, x30, [sp,
#FRAME-16]`? Because `stp`/`ldp` take a **7-bit signed immediate scaled by 8** — offsets from
−512 to +504 — and a function with about sixty SIL values (twenty statements) has a frame past
that: the assembler refuses the file. Pushing the record at offset 0 sidesteps the limit for any
frame size; `sub`/`add` take a 12-bit immediate, so a locals area above 4095 bytes is adjusted in
several steps (`adjust_sp`, given). Both are given code — you will meet them in concept 35, where
`x29` becomes the handle for reading stack-passed arguments.

Because all state lives in the frame, a `bl` (call) — which clobbers x0–x18 — is harmless:
nothing important is in a register across a call. That's the stack machine's other gift: calls
are trivially correct.

### Calls and the AAPCS64 convention

A function call lowers to: load arguments into `x0`, `x1`, … (the first eight arg registers), `bl
_callee`, then store `x0` (the return value) to the result's slot. A function definition spills its
incoming parameters (`x0`, `x1`, …) to their slots on entry, so the body can treat them like any
other value. Recursion needs nothing special — `fib` calling `fib` is just a `bl _fib`; each
activation has its own frame.

### `print` and the Apple variadic gotcha

`print(n)` calls libc's `printf("%lld\n", n)`. The format string goes in `x0` — but `n` is a
**variadic** argument, and here Apple's arm64 ABI diverges from the generic AAPCS64: **variadic
arguments are passed on the stack**, not in registers. So we store `n` at `[sp, #0]` (our reserved
scratch), put the format-string address in `x0`, and `bl _printf`. (On Linux arm64 the same code
would pass `n` in `x1`; this stack rule is Apple-specific, and getting it wrong prints garbage — a
classic first-native-backend bug.) The format string lives in a `__TEXT,__cstring` section,
addressed by the two-instruction `adrp x0, L@PAGE; add x0, x0, L@PAGEOFF` PC-relative pair.

### Comparisons, division, modulo

A few ARM64-isms the templates encode:

- a **comparison** (`a < b`) is two instructions: `cmp x9, x10` sets the condition flags, then
  `cset x9, lt` materializes `0`/`1` from them.
- **division** is `sdiv` (signed). There is **no modulo instruction**: `a % b` is `sdiv x11, x9,
  x10` (the quotient) then `msub x9, x11, x10, x9` (`x9 = x9 − x11*x10` — the remainder). Knowing
  the machine lacks an op and synthesizing it is the essence of instruction selection.
- a **constant** larger than 16 bits can't be one `mov`; it's built with `movz` + up to three
  `movk` (one 16-bit chunk at a time). `materialize` (given) handles this.

### What the backend refuses, and how

This concept adds **no diagnostics**: by the time SIL reaches isel the program has type-checked,
and every scalar SIL op has a template. What it does have is a *scope boundary*. v0 lowers
Int/Bool scalars, arithmetic, comparisons, branches, calls and `print`; a struct, enum, class,
array or closure instruction has no template yet. The rule for those is: emit a **visible
`; UNSUPPORTED instr for %v: …` comment** in the assembly, in the place the code would go — never
silently skip the instruction and never guess. The program still assembles, its scalar parts still
run, and `--emit-asm` shows exactly which ops are missing. A backend that miscompiles quietly is
worse than one that says what it cannot do; the comment is what the tests pin.

The only runtime failure in the subset is a `trap` terminator (a force-unwrap of `nil`, from
concept 13), which lowers to `brk #1` — SIGTRAP, exit 133, the same signal swiftc's traps raise.
The optional machinery around it is outside v0, so this is shape-tested, not run.

### Why lower the `-Onone` SIL?

We lower the **raw, memory-based** SIL (the `-Onone` path), not the optimized SSA form. Raw SIL has
**no block arguments** — control flow is plain `br`/`cond_br`, and variables already live in
`alloc_stack` slots — which maps directly onto the stack machine with zero phi/SSA handling. The
optimized SSA form (block args = φ-nodes) needs *parallel copies on edges* to lower, which is real
work; it arrives in concept 34, where register allocation makes the SSA form worth the trouble. v0
keeps the first backend simple and correct.

### How a real backend does it

LLVM's path is the same shape, industrialized: SelectionDAG / GlobalISel does instruction selection
(but with *maximal munch* — matching multi-node patterns like `a*b+c` → a single `madd`), then a
real register allocator, then scheduling, then encoding to bytes. Our v0 is "minimal munch" (one
SIL op at a time) emitting *text* (assembled by `as`); concept 33's exercise and concept 36 climb
toward pattern matching, and the regalloc ladder (34) is the big perf lever. The architecture —
select → allocate → schedule → encode — is exactly LLVM's; we're just doing each stage by hand.

> Oracle: there's no single `swift/lib` file for this (swiftc *is* LLVM here); the references are
> the LLVM AArch64 backend and Apple's *Writing ARM64 Code for Apple Platforms* (the calling
> convention, the variadic rule, PC-relative addressing).

## 3. Build it, step by step

You implement two functions in `isel.ml`. Given: the frame layout, `materialize dst n` (build a
constant), `load r v` / `store r v` (slot access), `lea_cstring` (string address), `epilogue ()`,
`cond_of` (comparison → condition code), and the whole `arm64.ml` IR + printer.

1. **`TODO(33a)` — `sel_instr v i`**: one ARM64 sequence per SIL op (§2 gives each sequence):
   literals → `materialize` + `store`; `load`/`store` → `ldr`/`str` through slots; `binop` →
   load-load-compute-store (with the `mod` = `sdiv`+`msub` and comparison = `cmp`+`cset` cases);
   `apply` → args into `x0…`, `bl _name`, store `x0`; `print` → the `printf` call with the
   variadic on the stack. Unsupported ops emit a visible `; UNSUPPORTED` comment. Two details
   the tests notice: a `func_ref` produces no code (its target is already in `funcrefs`, so the
   `apply` can be a direct `bl`), and an `alloc_stack` is only a comment — the slot is the
   variable.
2. **`TODO(33b)` — `sel_term t`**: `return` → load `x0` + `epilogue` (`@main`'s bare `return`
   puts 0 in `x0` first — the exit code); `br` → `b`; `cond_br` → `cmp #0` + `b.ne` + `b`;
   `trap`/`abort` → `brk #1`; `unreachable` → nothing.

Do 33a first, then 33b's `Return` arms: nothing prints until a function can end, so both cram
files stay `TODO` until then (§4). The answer key is `solution/isel.ml`; `make check-solution
C=phase8-arm64-backend/33-arm64-isel` runs the tests against it.

## 4. Test it

```bash
make lab C=phase8-arm64-backend/33-arm64-isel
```

Two cram files, one per hole, plus the unit suite and the three-way oracle — in the order you fill
the holes. One wrinkle is specific to this concept: `sel_instr` and `sel_term` are closures inside
`lower_func`, and a function cannot be printed without its `ret`, so nothing goes green until the
`return` arm of `sel_term` exists. Fill 33a, then 33b's `Return` arms, and both files light up
together; the remaining `sel_term` arms are what the branch cases check.

- `isel-instrs.t` — `--emit-asm`, one case per template: the literal (one `mov`) and the 2^62
  constant (`movz` + `movk`), `alloc_stack`/`store`/`load` through slots, each binop on x9/x10,
  `%` as `sdiv` + `msub`, the six condition codes of `cset`, `print(Bool)` via `csel`, a call's
  x0/x1 + `bl` + `str x0` and the callee's parameter spills, eight arguments filling x0–x7, and a
  struct lowering to `; UNSUPPORTED` comments.
- `isel-term.t` — the terminators, and the first programs that RUN natively: an empty `main`
  (frame, `mov x0, #0`, exit 0), `return` loading x0, `if`'s `cmp #0`/`b.ne`/`b`, the `while`
  back-edge, `for` with `break`/`continue`, `trap` as `brk #1`, recursive `fib`, a 40-statement
  `main` whose 1 KB frame still assembles, and Backend B agreeing with Backend A on `fib`.
- `test_isel.ml` (alcotest `isel`) — the same shapes in-process, grouped `frame` / `sel_instr
  (33a)` / `sel_term (33b)`, including the prologue pin (record at offset 0, no `stp`/`ldp` off 0).
- `oracle.t` — **the headline**: every program in `oracle-corpus.txt` (21 scalar programs: fib,
  collatz, primes, gcd, mutual recursion, nested loops, `break`/`continue`, short-circuit
  `&&`/`||` with side effects, eight-argument calls, 2^62 constants, `fact(20)`) is compiled by
  `swiftc -Onone`, by `./lab.exe build` (Backend A) and by `./lab.exe build --native` (Backend B);
  all three run and stdout + exit code must match. A refusal is reported as a refusal; when the
  native build dies on a `TODO(`, the loop stops so the file reads `TODO`, not as twenty
  divergences.

A hole you have not started shows as `TODO` with the list of what it will check; a hole in
progress shows `FAIL` with, under each failing case, what the test wants and what your code
printed. `DETAIL=1` forces the diffs for a `TODO` file too.

## 5. Benchmark it

Look at the asm for a hot loop and count the `ldr`/`str`: every iteration reloads the induction
variable and accumulator from the frame. That's the cost. Time a loop-heavy program built `--native`
(v0) against the same program through `clang -O0` and `swiftc -O` — v0 will be far behind, and that
gap is exactly what the register-allocation ladder closes in concept 34. Measuring it now sets the
baseline the ladder has to beat.

## 6. Exercises

1. **Immediate operands.** `x + 3` currently materializes `3` into a register first. ARM64's
   `add`/`sub`/`cmp` take a 12-bit immediate directly — emit `add x9, x9, #3` when the operand is a
   small `Int_lit`. (Your first peephole; concept 36 generalizes it.)
2. **Maximal munch.** Match `a*b + c` (a `binop add` whose operand is a `binop mul`) and emit a
   single `madd x9, xa, xb, xc`. One pattern, but it's the whole idea of pattern-matched isel.
3. **`tbz`/`cbz` for conditions.** `cond_br` currently does `cmp #0; b.ne; b`. When the condition is
   a comparison result, branch on the flags directly (`b.lt`, …); when it's `== 0`, use `cbz`.
4. **Spill fewer literals.** A value used exactly once, immediately, needn't get a slot — thread it
   in a register. (A taste of register allocation, by hand.)
5. **Real encoding.** Instead of asm text, encode a handful of instructions to their 32-bit machine
   words and emit a Mach-O object directly — the ladder's true top rung.

## 7. Recap & what's next

Instruction selection turns abstract SIL into concrete ARM64. v0 is a **stack machine**: a frame
slot per value, one template per op, load-compute-store. It's local, correct, and runs real
programs that match `swiftc` — with two backends now sharing one front end. Its weakness, the
load/store traffic, is the lever for everything next.

Next, **34-register-allocation** — the flagship Phase-8 concept and a runnable **ladder**: v0 stack
(this) → v1 linear-scan → v2 graph-coloring, each rung keeping more values in registers and beating
the last, the top rung approaching LLVM's own allocator. Then **35-mc-abi** (real frames & the full
AAPCS64), **36-peephole-sched**, **37-debug-info** — to **M8-core**.

## 8. Appendix — full solution

```ocaml
(* 33a — one template per SIL op (the stack machine) *)
let sel_instr (v : Sil.value) (i : Sil.instr) : unit =
  match i with
  | Sil.Int_lit n -> materialize (x 9) n; store (x 9) v
  | Sil.Bool_lit b -> materialize (x 9) (if b then 1 else 0); store (x 9) v
  | Sil.Func_ref _ -> ()                        (* the apply turns it into a direct bl *)
  | Sil.Alloc_stack name -> emit (Arm64.Comment (Printf.sprintf "alloc_stack %s" name))
  | Sil.Load a -> load (x 9) a; store (x 9) v
  | Sil.Store (src, a) -> load (x 9) src; store (x 9) a
  | Sil.Unop (Ast.Neg, a) -> load (x 9) a; emit (Arm64.Neg (x 9, x 9)); store (x 9) v
  | Sil.Binop (op, l, r) ->
      load (x 9) l; load (x 10) r;
      (match op with
      | Ast.Add -> emit (Arm64.Add (x 9, x 9, Arm64.R (x 10)))
      | Ast.Sub -> emit (Arm64.Sub (x 9, x 9, Arm64.R (x 10)))
      | Ast.Mul -> emit (Arm64.Mul (x 9, x 9, x 10))
      | Ast.Div -> emit (Arm64.Sdiv (x 9, x 9, x 10))
      | Ast.Mod -> emit (Arm64.Sdiv (x 11, x 9, x 10)); emit (Arm64.Msub (x 9, x 11, x 10, x 9))
      | Ast.And -> emit (Arm64.And (x 9, x 9, Arm64.R (x 10)))
      | Ast.Or  -> emit (Arm64.Orr (x 9, x 9, Arm64.R (x 10)))
      | _ -> emit (Arm64.Cmp (x 9, Arm64.R (x 10))); emit (Arm64.Cset (x 9, cond_of op)));
      store (x 9) v
  | Sil.Apply (callee, args) ->
      List.iteri (fun k a -> load (x k) a) args;
      emit (Arm64.Bl ("_" ^ Hashtbl.find funcrefs callee)); store (x 0) v
  | Sil.Print a -> (match vty a with
      | Types.TBool ->
          load (x 9) a;
          lea_cstring (x 11) (use_cstring "Ltrue" "true");
          lea_cstring (x 12) (use_cstring "Lfalse" "false");
          emit (Arm64.Cmp (x 9, Arm64.Imm 0)); emit (Arm64.Csel (x 9, x 11, x 12, Arm64.NE));
          emit (Arm64.Str (x 9, Arm64.SP, 0));
          lea_cstring (x 0) (use_cstring "Lfmt_str" "%s\n"); emit (Arm64.Bl "_printf")
      | _ ->
          load (x 9) a; emit (Arm64.Str (x 9, Arm64.SP, 0));
          lea_cstring (x 0) (use_cstring "Lfmt_int" "%lld\n"); emit (Arm64.Bl "_printf"))
  | other -> emit (Arm64.Comment ("UNSUPPORTED: " ^ Sil.string_of_instr f (v, other)))

(* 33b — terminators *)
let sel_term (t : Sil.term) : unit =
  match t with
  | Sil.Return (Some a) -> load (x 0) a; epilogue ()
  | Sil.Return None -> if is_main then materialize (x 0) 0; epilogue ()
  | Sil.Br (n, _) -> emit (Arm64.B (blabel n))
  | Sil.Cond_br (c, (tb, _), (eb, _)) ->
      load (x 9) c; emit (Arm64.Cmp (x 9, Arm64.Imm 0));
      emit (Arm64.Bcond (Arm64.NE, blabel tb)); emit (Arm64.B (blabel eb))
  | Sil.Trap _ | Sil.Abort _ -> emit (Arm64.Brk 1)
  | Sil.Unreachable -> ()
```

## 9. Exercise solutions

### 1 — immediate operands
In the `binop` template, special-case `r` being a small non-negative `Int_lit`: emit `Add (x9, x9,
Imm n)` instead of materializing `n` into `x10` first. ARM64's add/sub/cmp accept a 12-bit
unsigned immediate (optionally shifted by 12), so `n < 4096` qualifies. Saves a `mov` + a register.

### 2 — maximal munch
Before lowering a `binop add (l, r)`, peek: if `r` is itself a `binop mul (a, b)` whose result is
used only here, emit `madd x9, xa, xb, xl` (a fused multiply-add) in one instruction. This is
tree-pattern matching — the difference between "minimal munch" (one node) and "maximal munch"
(largest matching subtree), which is how production isel earns its name.

### 3 — tbz/cbz
Track when a `cond_br`'s condition value is *defined by* a comparison `cmp`. Instead of
materializing `0`/`1` (`cset`) and re-testing it (`cmp #0; b.ne`), branch on the original flags:
`b.lt label`. For an equality-to-zero test, `cbz x9, label`. Removes a `cset` and a `cmp` per
branch — common in tight loops.

### 4 — single-use values
A value produced and consumed by the very next instruction (e.g. `%9 = load; %10 = binop … %9 …`)
needn't be stored and reloaded — keep it in the scratch register. A tiny liveness check ("is this
value used again after the next instruction?") lets you skip the `str`/`ldr` pair. This is register
allocation in miniature, and motivates doing it *properly* in concept 34.

### 5 — real encoding
Each ARM64 instruction is a 32-bit word with fixed bit-fields (opcode, registers, immediate).
Encode, say, `add`/`ldr`/`str`/`ret`/`b` to their words, write a minimal Mach-O object with a
`__text` section and the right relocations, and link with `ld` directly — no `as`. This is the
backend's true bottom turtle, and where "assembly text" becomes "machine code."
```
